video.title: How Alcaraz Hits Harder Than Everyone

classification.reason: The coach provides executable technical cues and an against-the-wall drill to practice the wrist snap momentum handoff.

problem.title_as_question: How does Carlos Alcaraz hit harder than everyone else on the forehand?
problem.definition: Carlos Alcaraz achieves unmatched forehand racket head speed through an exceptionally efficient proximal-to-distal kinetic whip, transferring momentum from the trunk to the arm and from the arm into the racket.

quotes.text: Carlos Alcarez's forehand is more biomechanically powerful than everyone else's.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The forehand is a proximal to distal whip. How much energy can you get from your butt into your racket head?
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: in order to have Carlos's forehand, you have to hand your momentum from the trunk to the arm and then hand as much of it as you can from the arm to the racket.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: in the early rotation phase. Look how far the trunk turns. Look how fast the trunk turns. And then from here until contact, look how little the trunk moves.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And you can see the handoff because right before contact, that trunk is almost frozen. This is what Federra did. This is what we're going to see Nadal do later.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: and then how slow it's moving right before contact. That's how much of that energy they actually sent into the arm. This is where we're going to see Nakushima leak later.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Next, let's talk about the arm to racket handoff. So early the arm is actually moving faster than the racket. See how the racket is actually getting stuck behind the arm? That's what we want.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And now from here that racket is overtaking the arm. So here the racket and the arm are moving the same speed and here the racket is overtaking the arm.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The wrist simply isn't strong enough to act as a perfect whip. To be honest, Carlos' wrist is insanely strong. He goes from 95, maybe even 80 degrees of lag out to like 160, 170.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: But, going from something like 90° to 135° is very, very doable and will make your forehand much better. That's how you crack the arm's momentum into the racket head.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: You want everything to fall off to your left in order to reverse the whip, in order to hand the momentum from your racket back off into your trunk to take speed away and deload your wrist and de load
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: not quite as explosive early as Alcarez and then just leaks a little more of that rotation through the contact than Alcarez does.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: See how that trunk is laser still? So, you know, if you could develop Nakushima's forehand, that would be amazing. But then, you know, Alcarez is just at that next level of perfection
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: When you swing through the ball close to your body like this, it's not as natural for the hand to pull back on the handle and create that little whipping effect that causes the momentum to go into the racket.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: And that's why you want to use more space. And that's one thing we've really helped clients with is creating the space that makes that handoff natural.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The other thing here is he is in either neutral or negative balance. He is falling back just a little bit while hitting this shot.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The truth is if you can get your knees and your quads and your your feet involved by leaning in while using your rotation, you can get even more force
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: First, I want to watch trunk just like Algarz. Extremely explosive and then frozen. I'm going to slow it down for you. Ready? Extremely explosive. And then absolutely frozen.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: When you swing out away from your body, your hand will just naturally tug on that handle. You won't have to like think about it and do this on purpose. It'll feel so comfortable.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: But when you're on the run, you need to hand off 100% of your force into the racket because you don't have that much force to start with.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: Now I have found that that most distal handoff from the arm through the wrist into the racket. It it trips a lot of people up and it's just straight up missing from a lot of forehands.
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: The good news is you can just practice using your hand, using just a tiny bit of elastic snap from the wrist to hit against the wall. Don't over crack your wrist. Don't overdo it
quotes.speaker: coach

quotes.text: We take people through a lot of these kind of progressions to make these handoffs intuitive and like not so scary and superhuman like they look when Alcas does it.
quotes.speaker: coach

symptoms.description: The trunk continues rotating through contact rather than abruptly decelerating and freezing.
The racket head fails to whip through and overtake the arm, lacking pop and control.
The shot lacks heavy pace and depth when on the run or when unable to set the feet.

causes.statement: The player fails to freeze or decelerate the trunk right before contact, leaking rotational momentum instead of transferring it into the arm.
The arm-to-racket momentum handoff fails because the racket does not overtake the arm through distal wrist lag and snap.
Swinging too close to the body crowds the contact point and prevents the hand from naturally tugging back on the handle to whip the racket.
The player hits from neutral or negative balance and falls backward instead of leaning in to recruit the feet, knees, and quads.

angles.summary: The forehand operates as a proximal-to-distal whip where kinetic momentum must transfer sequentially from the hips and trunk to the arm and finally to the racket.
Top forehands exhibit an explosive trunk turn early that suddenly appears completely frozen and stone-still right before contact.
Players often assume they should keep spinning the torso through the shot, but continuing to rotate through contact actually leaks power.
Rafael Nadal and Carlos Alcaraz achieve extreme racket head speed out of defensive corners because their nearly 100% efficient handoffs maximize force without setting feet.
Swinging out away from the body creates a comfortable feeling where the hand naturally tugs on the racket handle without having to force it consciously.

solutions.summary: Allow your body to fall off to the left during the follow-through to reverse the whip and deload the wrist and arm.
Create more space by swinging out away from the body so the hand can naturally tug on the handle.
Lean into the shot while rotating to recruit the feet, knees, and quads rather than falling backward.
Hit against a wall using just the hand with a small amount of elastic wrist snap back-to-front without over-cracking the wrist.
